metadata.title: High-Quality Teacher Professional Development and Classroom Teaching Practices (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data across 35 educational systems/economies and estimates relationships between teacher-reported professional development (TPD) features and teacher-reported classroom teaching practices. The methodology section specifies an ordinal regression model with school fixed effects (i.e., using within-school variation across teachers) and includes teacher background characteristics as controls, but it does not report the specific TALIS sampling/replicate weight variables or whether they were applied in estimation. Because the paper is an OECD analysis using TALIS microdata, analysts would typically use TALIS sampling weights and appropriate variance estimation for complex survey design when producing population-representative inferences; however, this manuscript does not document weight usage. The paper also applies questionnaire filtering logic implied by the TALIS TPD module (teachers who did not participate in any professional development during the last 12 months are directed to a later question), and it recodes Likert-type responses into ordered categories for the ordinal regression.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not model cognitive achievement scores with TALIS plausible values; instead, the dependent variables are Likert-scaled teacher-reported frequencies of classroom teaching practices and the key explanatory variables are TPD features derived from teacher questionnaire items. As a result, plausible values handling is not applicable to the reported outcomes. The manuscript also does not describe a missing-data strategy for the regression analyses (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), which is a reporting gap for transparency, especially because survey nonresponse can affect both TPD exposure and teaching-practice items.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data for the 35 countries and economies with available data. The analysis is restricted to teachers nested within schools and estimates school fixed-effects ordinal regression models for each of the 10 classroom teaching practice outcomes, using within-school variation across teachers. The paper conditions on the TALIS TPD questionnaire design (teachers who did not participate in any professional development during the last 12 months follow the questionnaire skip/response structure for the TPD module). Likert-type teaching-practice items are recoded into four ordered frequency categories (Never/almost never; Occasionally; Frequently; In all/nearly all lessons) for ordinal regression.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper analyzes TALIS 2013 teacher questionnaire data from 35 educational systems/economies to examine whether “high-quality” teacher professional development (TPD) is associated with teachers’ reported classroom teaching practices. The study distinguishes TPD content foci (subject matter, pedagogy, curriculum) from delivery features (collaboration, collective participation, active learning, and duration), including an overall index of effective professional development. Ten classroom teaching practices are operationalized as Likert-scaled ordinal outcomes reflecting frequency of reported implementation over the prior year, and the relationships are estimated using school fixed-effects ordinal regression models with teacher background controls. Results are presented as percentage changes in odds associated with one standard deviation increases in TPD exposure, and the paper also reports cross-national prevalence gaps by gender and initial training completion. A key limitation noted is that student outcomes are not included, so the analysis cannot establish whether TPD improves learning effectiveness beyond associations with reported practices.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because this OECD/TALIS analysis uses ordinal regression with school fixed effects rather than machine-learning predictive modeling. The paper reports cross-national associations (odds ratios/percentage changes) between TPD features and ordinal teaching-practice outcomes, so there are no ML algorithms, PV handling, or predictive performance metrics to extract. Consequently, main_findings is left empty per the framework rule for official OECD/IEA-style reports without student-level ML prediction outputs.
